name: Framelink

hlido_opinion.headline: A Figma-to-code MCP server that deliberately sends descriptive data rather than generated React — and publishes an honest, self-deprecating comparison against Figma’s own MCP.
hlido_opinion.body: Framelink solves a narrow problem well and explains its reasoning better than most tools in this category bother to. It pulls layouts, styles and components straight out of Figma into a coding agent's context over MCP, so the agent stops working from screenshots. The interesting decision is what it sends: descriptive JSON ('this element has a 1px border and 16px padding') rather than the prescriptive React and Tailwind that Figma's official MCP emits. The vendor's argument is that prescriptive output poisons the context — the model mimics auto-generated structure with arbitrary pixel values instead of using your components and conventions, so you end up refactoring the AI's output rather than using it. That is a real, specific failure mode, and the page shows the two outputs side by side rather than asserting the difference. Adoption backs the design: 15,000+ GitHub stars, and it advertises working with Cursor, Claude Code, VS Code, Codex and OpenCode. What earns Framelink credit beyond the engineering is the footnote under its own comparison table: the ~25% size advantage is marked '*Based on a few admittedly haphazard tests. I should probably do more.' A vendor that labels its own benchmark as weak is telling you where the evidence ends, and we would rather rate that than a confident unsourced number. The limits are the flip side of the focus: this is a single-purpose connector with no pricing or commercial-support story on the surface, the paid tier is a waitlist ('Special features coming soon. Sign up for early access'), and the size and quality claims remain the vendor's own haphazard tests, not an independent measurement.

tier_rationale: STEADY (80) because the design choice is technically specific and demonstrated side-by-side rather than asserted, adoption is substantial at 15,000+ stars across every major MCP host, and the vendor labels the weakness of its own benchmark in plain language — an honesty signal we weight. Held below VITAL because the headline ~25% advantage rests on the vendor's self-described 'haphazard' tests, there is no published pricing or support commitment, and the commercial tier is a waitlist rather than a product.
what_it_does_well: Sends descriptive design data instead of prescriptive generated code, so the agent uses your components and conventions
Preserves style names and represents nested components accurately rather than flattening them
Publishes a direct side-by-side comparison against Figma’s official MCP instead of asserting superiority
Explicitly labels its own benchmark as weak — "a few admittedly haphazard tests" — rather than presenting it as rigorous
Broad host support: Cursor, Claude Code, VS Code, Codex, OpenCode and other MCP clients
15,000+ GitHub stars indicates real adoption for a single-purpose connector
what_it_fails_at: The ~25% output-size advantage is the vendor’s own self-described haphazard testing, not an independent measurement
No published pricing, licence terms or support commitment on the reviewed surface
Paid capability is a waitlist ("Special features coming soon") rather than a shipped tier
Single-purpose by design — it does Figma-to-context and nothing else
Output quality still depends entirely on the downstream agent; Framelink supplies context, not code
best_for: Teams whose coding agent produces design-faithful markup but drifts from their own component conventions
Anyone currently pasting Figma screenshots into a coding agent
Design-system codebases where preserved style names matter more than generated markup
not_recommended_for: Teams that want generated React/Tailwind handed to them directly — Figma’s own MCP is the prescriptive option
Buyers who need a commercial support agreement or published SLA

compared_to.verdict_diff: Cursor is the agent host; Framelink is a context source that plugs into it over MCP. They are complementary rather than alternatives — Framelink improves what Cursor sees about a design, it does not replace the editor.

Both are MCP context servers that feed a coding agent evidence instead of guesses. Octocode sources cited context from GitHub, npm and local code; Framelink sources it from Figma design files. Pick by where your missing context lives.

agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: Connect the Framelink MCP server to any MCP host (Cursor, Claude Code, VS Code, Codex, OpenCode). The agent then calls it to retrieve descriptive layout, style and component data for a Figma node, and generates code in whatever language the user asks for. It is a pure context provider — the agent does the generation.

marking_signal.note: Developer context server for design-to-code; it produces structured design data for an agent, not public-facing synthetic media, so machine-readable output marking is not an applicable obligation here.
